sections.b:
Matthew 24–25 is the longest form of the discourse. Matthew follows Mark 13 for the warnings and signs (24:1–36), adds sayings shared with Luke 17 and 12 about Noah, the thief and the two slaves (24:37–51), and closes with three scenes found only or chiefly in Matthew: the ten young women, the talents and the sheep and goats (25:1–46). The disciples' question is wider than in Mark: "What sign will mark your coming and the completion of the age?" (24:3). Matthew uses parousia, "coming," four times in this chapter and nowhere else among the Gospels.

Readers divide the discourse in different ways. Many see a turn at 24:36, from "those days," which have signs, to "that day," which no one knows. Preterists read most of it as the war of AD 66–70; futurists read it as a future tribulation and return; many read a near fulfillment in AD 70 that previews the final one. On every reading, more than half the discourse is about how to live while waiting.

common: The Temple's fall in AD 70 fulfilled at least part of the discourse.
The parables of 24:45–25:30 are about being faithful while Christ's return is delayed.
uncommon: The whole discourse, including the coming on the clouds, was fulfilled in AD 70 (full preterism).
The fig tree of 24:32 is the modern state of Israel.

claude.title: From a building to a person
claude.body: The discourse opens with Jesus leaving a Temple he has declared deserted and ends with the King saying "you did it for me" (25:40). Matthew may be tracing an arc from the place where God's presence was sought to the persons in whom Christ is now met. See the chapter page for Matthew 24.

sections.b: Jesus names "the abomination of desolation" spoken of by Daniel and says that when it stands "in a holy place," those in Judea must flee to the hills (Matthew 24:15–16). Matthew adds the reference to Daniel; Mark has the strange masculine "standing where he must not stand" (Mark 13:14), and Luke speaks instead of Jerusalem surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20). Readers have identified it with the Zealots' bloodshed in the Temple in 67–68, the Roman standards set up in the Temple court and worshiped in August 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6.6.1), a future Antichrist in a rebuilt temple (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4), or every power that takes God's place. The aside "the one who reads this should think about what it means" suggests that the first readers were expected to recognize it.
sections.refs: Matthew 24:15–16; Mark 13:14; Luke 21:20; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–4

sections.b: Jesus' disciples will be handed over to thlipsis, suffering (Matthew 24:9), and after the abomination appears there will be "great suffering," worse than any since the world began (Matthew 24:21), an echo of Daniel 12:1. Josephus described the siege of Jerusalem in words much like these. Preterists read it as the war of AD 66–70; futurists as a future great tribulation, often the last seven years of Daniel 9:27; idealists as the suffering of God's people in every age. The days will be cut short for the sake of the chosen (Matthew 24:22), and immediately after them the sky goes dark and the Son of Man appears (Matthew 24:29–30). Revelation 7:14 uses the same phrase for those who come out of "the great suffering."

Matthew 24:40–41 pictures two men in a field and two women at a mill: one is taken along, one is left behind. Pre-tribulation teachers such as Tim LaHaye, and the Left Behind novels, read this as the rapture. But the verse just before compares the coming to the flood, which "carried them all off" (Matthew 24:39), so many scholars, including dispensational scholars such as John Walvoord and Louis Barbieri, read the ones taken as taken in judgment. Others read it as the gathering of the chosen at Christ's single return (Matthew 24:31). The verb for "taken along" (paralambanō) is the one used for Jesus taking his disciples to himself in John 14:3.

Only Matthew among the Gospels uses parousia, the word for a ruler's arrival, for Jesus' coming (Matthew 24:3, 27, 37, 39). He says it will be as public as lightning (24:27), as sudden as the flood (24:37–39) and as unexpected as a thief (24:43), and that no one, not even the Son, knows the day (24:36). The Son of Man will come on the clouds with power and glory (24:30), gather his chosen with a great trumpet (24:31), and sit on the throne of his glory to judge the nations (25:31–46). Jesus' answer to "when?" is mostly practical: stay awake, be ready, be faithful.

sections.h: The Son of Man on the clouds and on the throne
sections.b: In Matthew 24:30 Jesus joins Daniel 7:13 with Zechariah 12:10: the tribes of the earth mourn and see the Son of Man coming on the clouds. Revelation 1:7 makes the same combination. In Daniel the one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive a kingdom, so some scholars (N. T. Wright, R. T. France) read Jesus' words as his vindication and enthronement, seen in the events of AD 70; most readers take them as his return to earth. In Matthew 25:31 the Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory and is called "the King," as in 1 Enoch's Parables, where the Son of Man sits on the throne of glory to judge.
sections.refs: Matthew 24:27; Matthew 24:30; Matthew 25:31–34; Daniel 7:13–14; Zechariah 12:10; Revelation 1:7; 1 Enoch 62:2–5

sections.b: Jesus leaves the Temple after declaring it deserted (Matthew 23:38) and foretells that not one stone will be left on another (Matthew 24:1–2). Herod's Temple, begun about 20 BC and finished only around AD 63, was burned in August AD 70 and the city pulled down (Josephus, Jewish War 6–7). The prediction was used against Jesus at his trial (Matthew 26:61) and mocked at the cross (Matthew 27:40). For Matthew's readers the loss of the Temple did not mean the loss of God's presence: Jesus is Immanuel (Matthew 1:23), and he meets people in "the least" of his brothers (Matthew 25:40).

The same schools that read Revelation in different ways read the discourse on the Mount of Olives differently too. Partial preterists read 24:4–35 as the war of AD 66–70, stressing "this generation" (24:34), and read 24:36 onward as the final return. Full preterists place all of chapters 24–25 in AD 70. Futurists, especially dispensationalists, read it as a future tribulation centered on Israel. Idealists see the pattern of every age. Historicists, such as early Adventists, saw the signs of 24:29 fulfilled in events of the 1700s and 1800s. Others, such as John Chrysostom and Calvin, see a double fulfillment: AD 70 first, the end later. Another view, common among historians since Albert Schweitzer, holds that Jesus or his followers expected the end within a lifetime.

Matthew 24:34 is the Gospels' sharpest time-statement: "this generation will not be gone before all these things happen." Elsewhere in Matthew "this generation" means Jesus' own hearers (Matthew 11:16; Matthew 23:36). Readers take it to mean the people of Jesus' day, with fulfillment in AD 70; the generation that sees the signs at the end; the Jewish people; or humanity. Albert Schweitzer concluded that Jesus was mistaken, and C. S. Lewis called it the most embarrassing verse in the Bible while noting that the next sentence confesses the Son's ignorance of the day (24:36). The parables that follow assume a delay (24:48; 25:5; 25:19).
sections.refs: Matthew 24:34–36; Matthew 24:48; Matthew 25:5; Matthew 25:19; Matthew 16:28; Matthew 10:23

sections.b: Matthew ends Jesus' teaching with a cluster of parables about the time before the master returns: the fig tree (Matthew 24:32–35), the thief (24:43–44), the faithful and the evil slave (24:45–51), the ten young women (25:1–13) and the talents (25:14–30), followed by the judgment scene of the sheep and the goats (25:31–46). Each divides people into two groups and turns on what they did while the master or groom was away. The talents has a cousin in Luke's parable of the minas (Luke 19:11–27), told to a crowd who thought the kingdom would appear at once.

In the judgment scene of Matthew 25:31–46 the King identifies himself with the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner. Mercy shown to "one of these brothers of mine, even the least of them" is mercy shown to him; mercy withheld is withheld from him. These six acts, with burying the dead from Tobit, became the corporal works of mercy in Catholic and Orthodox teaching. Jewish teaching already called such deeds the way to imitate God (Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 14a). Whether "the least" are every needy person or Jesus' needy disciples is debated (see the card at Matthew 25).

sections.h: "The eternal fire made ready for the devil"
sections.b: Matthew 25:41 is the clearest link between Jesus' teaching and Revelation's lake of fire: the fire was "made ready for the devil and his angels," just as in Revelation 20:10 the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. The kingdom was made ready for the blessed from the founding of the world (Matthew 25:34), but the fire was not made for human beings. Matthew 25:46 sets "eternal punishment" beside "eternal life," with the same adjective, which Augustine used to argue that the punishment is endless. Those who hold that the wicked are finally destroyed read "eternal" as describing the result.

sections.h: The judgment of the nations and the thousand years
sections.b: Dispensational writers place the judgment of the sheep and goats (Matthew 25:31–46) at the start of the millennium: living Gentile nations are judged when Christ returns, and the sheep enter his thousand-year kingdom, with the great white throne judgment of the dead a thousand years later (Revelation 20:11–15). Amillennial and postmillennial readers, and the creeds of the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed churches, see one general judgment at the end, the same scene as Revelation 20.

In Matthew 25:32 the Son of Man separates people as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. The image comes from Ezekiel 34, where God himself judges "between sheep and sheep, between rams and male goats" and promises to set his servant David over them as shepherd (Ezekiel 34:17, 23). The shepherd who cares for the flock is also the one who sorts it.

sections.h: The groom who comes at midnight
sections.b: In the parable of the ten young women (Matthew 25:1–13) the kingdom is a wedding, and the groom, delayed until midnight, is Christ. Matthew has already called Jesus the groom (Matthew 9:15) and the kingdom a king's wedding feast (Matthew 22:1–14). Revelation completes the picture with the wedding of the Lamb and the bride made ready (Revelation 19:7–9). Some early witnesses add "and the bride" in Matthew 25:1, but the Greek manuscripts overwhelmingly leave her out.

The disciples ask about "the completion of the age" (Matthew 24:3), Matthew's phrase for the close of the present age (Matthew 13:39–49; Matthew 28:20). Jesus answers that wars and earthquakes are only "the start of the labor pains" (24:8), the Jewish image of the sufferings before the new age, and that the end will come after the good news is proclaimed in the whole world (24:14).
